1.title: The Beginning of the Gospel
1.context: Mark opens with a headline and a quotation. The messenger line is from Malachi and the voice line from Isaiah; Mark credits the pair to Isaiah, the greater prophet, as ancient writers often did when joining texts.
1.question: What does it change for you that the story starts with a promise centuries old rather than with the events themselves?

1.title: A Baptism of Repentance
1.context: John's dress and diet echo the prophet Elijah (2 Kings 1:8). Baptism in the Jordan was a washing of repentance offered to Israel itself, not only to converts from outside.
1.question: What would it look like for you to go out to the river, so to speak, instead of waiting to be found?

1.title: One More Powerful Than I
1.context: Untying sandals was a slave's task; John ranks himself below it. In Mark, John promises a baptism with the Holy Spirit; the fire Matthew adds to the saying is not in Mark's wording.
1.question: Where are you tempted to point at yourself when you were meant to point past yourself?

1.title: You Are My Beloved Son
1.context: Jesus comes to the baptism from Nazareth with no introduction. The voice addresses him directly, 'You are My beloved Son,' where Matthew's wording speaks of him in the third person.
1.question: What does the Father's pleasure in Jesus, spoken before Jesus has done any public work, say to your own need to earn approval?

1.title: Driven into the Wilderness
1.context: Mark's verb is stronger than Matthew's: the Spirit drives Jesus out. Mark gives no dialogue of temptation, only forty days, Satan, wild animals, and ministering angels held side by side.
1.question: When have you experienced testing and attending care in the same season?

2.title: The Time Is Fulfilled
2.context: Mark dates the sermon by John's arrest. The word gospel in the ancient world also announced a king's victory or accession; Mark takes it up for the kingdom of God.
2.question: What part of Jesus' short sermon, repent and believe, is hardest for you to act on today?

2.title: Fishers of Men
2.context: Simon and Andrew, James and John were working fishermen on the Sea of Galilee, not students in a school. Mark stresses the immediacy of their leaving: nets, boat, father, and hired men.
2.question: What is the net, the ordinary task or security, that a call from Jesus would ask you to set down first?

2.title: A New Teaching with Authority
2.context: Capernaum becomes Jesus' base in Mark's early chapters. The scribes taught by citing authorities; the crowd hears Jesus speak as an authority himself.
2.question: When has Jesus' teaching unsettled you in a way that turned out to be good for you?

2.title: The Whole Town at the Door
2.context: The Sabbath day's healings wait until sunset, when the Sabbath rest ends. Jesus' predawn prayer and refusal to stay for the crowds set the pattern: the mission moves town to town.
2.question: How do you respond when people's expectations of you crowd out the purpose you believe you were given?

2.title: I Am Willing
2.context: Lepers lived cut off from worship and touch (Leviticus 13-14). Jesus touches the man before he is clean, reversing the expected direction of contagion.
2.question: Whose untouchability, in your world, might Jesus cross a boundary to end?

3.title: Through the Roof
3.context: Houses in Capernaum had flat roofs of beams and packed earth that could be dug through. Jesus addresses the paralytic's sins before his legs, to the scribes' silent outrage.
3.question: Which do you find yourself asking God for more often, relief of circumstances or forgiveness, and why?

3.title: Authority on Earth
3.context: Son of Man is Jesus' usual name for himself in Mark, drawn from Daniel 7. The healing is staged as evidence for the invisible claim about forgiving sins.
3.question: What visible evidence of grace in your life supports trusting God with the invisible parts?

3.title: A Doctor for the Sick
3.context: Tax collectors worked for Rome and were classed with sinners by religious society. Table fellowship was acceptance; eating with such people was the scandal, even more than calling Levi.
3.question: Who is at your table that your reputation might prefer not to be seen with, and what does Jesus' example say about it?

3.title: New Wine, New Wineskins
3.context: The bridegroom saying is the first hint of Jesus' death in Mark. Unshrunk cloth and new wine picture the kingdom's newness bursting arrangements built for the old.
3.question: Where are you trying to patch something God may be asking you to replace?

3.title: Lord of the Sabbath
3.context: Jesus cites David eating the consecrated bread (1 Samuel 21). The withered-hand healing closes the sequence, and the Pharisees' alliance with the Herodians, normally enemies, shows how early the opposition hardened.
3.question: When has doing good on the wrong day, or in the wrong way, drawn criticism you had to accept anyway?

4.title: You Are the Son of God
4.context: The crowd comes from as far as Idumea and the region of Tyre and Sidon. The unclean spirits' confessions are silenced throughout Mark, a pattern often called the messianic secret.
4.question: Why do you think Jesus refuses testimony about himself from the spirit world, even when it is accurate?

4.title: He Appointed Twelve
4.context: The twelve are appointed first to be with him, then to be sent. Mark's list ends with Judas and his future attached, the only list in the Gospels that labels him at his appointment.
4.question: What does it mean for your own life that being with Jesus is named before being sent by him?

4.title: Out of His Mind
4.context: The family scene and the scribes' charge arrive together. Beelzebul was a name for the prince of demons, derived from a Philistine god's title.
4.question: When has following Jesus made you look foolish or worse to people whose opinion matters to you?

4.title: Binding the Strong Man
4.context: The strong-man picture explains the exorcisms: a house is being plundered because its owner has been bound. The warning about blasphemy against the Spirit answers the charge that Jesus works by Satan's power.
4.question: How do you guard against calling something evil that God is actually doing, just because it arrives in an unexpected form?

4.title: Who Are My Mother and My Brothers?
4.context: Jesus redefines family around doing God's will, with his mother and brothers standing outside the door. The saying is about the priority of the new family, not a rejection of the old one.
4.question: What has the family of faith given you that blood family could not, and what has it cost?

5.title: The Sower and the Soils
5.context: Sowing before plowing was common in ancient Palestine, which explains seed on paths and rock. The yields of thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold far exceed a normal harvest.
5.question: Which soil best describes your hearing of God's word in this season, and what makes you say so?

5.title: The Mystery of the Kingdom
5.context: The Isaiah quotation (Isaiah 6:9-10) describes hearers who see without perceiving. Jesus explains this parable fully, making it the key to the others: the variable is the hearing, not the seed.
5.question: What most often chokes the word in you: worry, wealth's deceit, or the desire for other things?

5.title: The Seed Growing Secretly
5.context: The growing-seed parable is found only in Mark. The farmer's ignorance is part of the point: the kingdom's growth does not depend on the sower understanding or managing it.
5.question: Where do you need to trust a growth you cannot see or speed up?

5.title: The Smallest of All Seeds
5.context: The mustard seed proverbially was the smallest seed, yet its plant could reach ten feet or more. Mark notes Jesus taught in parables as the people could understand, explaining privately to his disciples.
5.question: What small beginning in your life might God intend to grow beyond all proportion?

6.title: Who Is This?
6.context: Fishing boats on the Sea of Galilee could be swamped quickly by winds funneled through the hills. The disciples' question after the calm becomes the Gospel's central question.
6.question: When has God answered your fear in a way that left you with a bigger question about him?

6.title: My Name Is Legion
6.context: The Gerasenes were a largely Gentile region east of the sea, which explains the pig herd. A Roman legion numbered several thousand; the name pictures an occupying army inside one man.
6.question: What does the townspeople's fear at a restored man, and their request that Jesus leave, expose about what people will trade for peace and quiet?

6.title: Go Home to Your Own People
6.context: The freed man becomes the first missionary to the Decapolis, the Ten Cities. In the same scene, the woman who touches Jesus' cloak had spent twelve years and all her money under physicians (Luke adds his own note; Mark reports her worsening plainly).
6.question: When has Jesus sent you back to your own people rather than onward to somewhere new?

6.title: Talitha Koum
6.context: Mark preserves Jesus' Aramaic words here and at the cross. Professional mourners were customary at funerals; the strict order of silence follows a raising witnessed by only the parents and three disciples.
6.question: What dead hope of yours would you need courage to let Jesus take by the hand?

7.title: Isn't This the Carpenter?
7.context: Nazareth calls Jesus by his trade and his mother's name, an unusual form that may itself carry a slight. Mark is the only Gospel that calls Jesus himself the carpenter.
7.question: How does familiarity with Jesus, his stories, his people, dull your amazement at him?

7.title: Amazed at Their Unbelief
7.context: The sending instructions create dependence on hospitality. Shaking dust off the feet was a visible sign of separation from a place that refused the message.
7.question: What has Jesus asked you to attempt with less equipment and security than you wanted?

7.title: John, Whom I Beheaded
7.context: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee as Rome's client. His marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife, violated Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21. Mark's portrait of Herod, fearing John, perplexed, yet listening gladly, is the fullest of any Gospel.
7.question: Where are you, like Herod, gladly listening to a word you are not obeying?

7.title: The Head of John the Baptist
7.context: Birthday banquets for client kings mixed festivity with displays of power; an oath before guests was nearly impossible to retract without shame. John's burial by his disciples quietly foreshadows Jesus' own.
7.question: What have you seen an oath, a promise, or a public image pressure someone into doing against their conscience?

8.title: Sheep Without a Shepherd
8.context: The phrase reaches back to Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34, where Israel's failed leaders leave the flock shepherdless. Jesus answers the need first with teaching, then with bread.
8.question: When has God interrupted your rest with someone else's need, and how did you respond?

8.title: You Give Them Something to Eat
8.context: Two hundred denarii was roughly two hundred days' wages. The orderly companies on the grass recall both an army and a flock, and the twelve baskets of leftovers exceed the five loaves that began the meal.
8.question: What little do you keep handing back to God as proof a thing cannot be done?

8.title: It Is I; Do Not Be Afraid
8.context: The fourth watch is between 3 and 6 in the morning. Mark's note that Jesus intended to pass by them echoes God's passing by Moses and Elijah in the Old Testament; the disciples' terror answers it.
8.question: What has it taken for you to recognize Jesus in the middle of the storm rather than after it?

8.title: The Fringe of His Cloak
8.context: The fringe or tassel of a cloak carried religious meaning (Numbers 15:38). Mark's summary verses compress whole regions of ministry into a few lines between his larger stories.
8.question: Where do you see people today reaching for the smallest possible contact with Jesus, and what happens to them?

9.title: You Nullify the Word of God
9.context: Corban was a vow dedicating property to God, which could be used to withhold support from parents while keeping use of the property for life. Jesus cites Isaiah 29:13 against the practice.
9.question: Is there a rule you keep that quietly excuses you from a plainer duty God has given?

9.title: What Comes Out of a Man
9.context: The saying relocates defilement from what is eaten to what is produced by the heart. Mark's parenthesis, that Jesus declared all foods clean, is the narrator's own explanation for his readers.
9.question: Which item in Jesus' list from the heart most needs your attention right now?

9.title: Even the Dogs Eat the Crumbs
9.context: Tyre was Gentile territory. The exchange about children and dogs uses a household word for dogs, and the woman answers inside the picture rather than resenting it, the only person in Mark to prevail in argument with Jesus.
9.question: How do you respond when God's first answer to your prayer sounds like a refusal?

9.title: Ephphatha
9.context: Jesus heals the deaf man privately with touch, spittle, and a sigh, means that look strange until they are read as a language the man could understand. Mark keeps the Aramaic word and translates it.
9.question: What has God used, that looked undignified or small, to open something closed in you?

10.title: Seven Loaves for Four Thousand
10.context: This feeding takes place in Gentile territory, following the Decapolis ministry. The word for baskets here differs from chapter 6, a large woven basket, and the leftovers fill seven.
10.question: Why do you think Jesus repeats the feeding miracle with the same disciples who saw the first one?

10.title: No Sign Will Be Given
10.context: Dalmanutha is an otherwise unknown place on the western shore. The demand for a sign from heaven comes right after a feeding, and Jesus' deep sigh answers it before his words do.
10.question: What sign, if any, are you still asking for before you will trust what God has already shown you?

10.title: Do You Still Not Understand?
10.context: Leaven pictured something small that spreads through everything. The disciples can recite both feedings' numbers exactly; the failure Mark records is of understanding, not memory.
10.question: What facts about God's faithfulness can you recite that have not yet become understanding?

10.title: Like Trees Walking Around
10.context: This is the only healing in the Gospels that happens in two stages. Mark places it at the hinge of his book, right before Peter's confession, like a living picture of the disciples' partial sight.
10.question: Where is your sight of Jesus real but still blurred, and what would the second touch be?

11.title: Who Do You Say I Am?
11.context: Caesarea Philippi, near the sources of the Jordan, was a center of pagan worship and imperial cult. Peter's confession here is the turning point of Mark's Gospel.
11.question: If Jesus asked you the question directly today, what would your answer add to the one you learned from others?

11.title: Get Behind Me, Satan
11.context: Mark says Jesus taught the suffering openly, not in parables. The cross saying was spoken to the crowd as well as the disciples, and the cross was Rome's public instrument of shame.
11.question: What does taking up a cross look like in your ordinary week, as opposed to in theory?

11.title: Listen to Him
11.context: Moses and Elijah represent the Law and the Prophets. The cloud and the voice repeat the baptism's announcement, now addressed to the disciples with a command to listen.
11.question: What word of Jesus do you most need to listen to rather than argue with?

11.title: Elijah Has Indeed Come
11.context: The scribes taught from Malachi 4 that Elijah would come before the day of the Lord. Jesus identifies Elijah's coming with John's fate, and lets the disciples draw the line to his own.
11.question: How do the fates of God's messengers prepare you for the way God himself was treated?

12.title: Help My Unbelief
12.context: The father's prayer has become one of the most quoted in the Gospels because it holds belief and unbelief in one sentence. Mark includes details of the boy's condition the other accounts shorten.
12.question: What would your own version of the father's prayer say, honestly, today?

12.title: Except by Prayer
12.context: Some manuscripts add 'and fasting' here; the BSB prints 'prayer.' The second passion prediction follows immediately, and Mark notes the disciples' fear of asking about it.
12.question: Where might God be inviting you from assumption about your own spiritual competence back to prayer?

12.title: The Last of All and Servant of All
12.context: The argument about greatness happens on the road right after the prediction of the cross. Jesus uses a child, who had no status in the ancient world, as the measure of welcome.
12.question: Who is the child, the person of no advantage to you, whose welcome would measure your place in the kingdom?

12.title: A Cup of Water and a Millstone
12.context: The outsider exorcist scene answers John's exclusiveness; the millstone warning protects the little ones of the previous scene. Salt in the ancient world preserved and purified, and the saying ends in peace within the company.
12.question: What stumbling block in your own life needs the surgeon's sentence rather than management?

13.title: What God Has Joined Together
13.context: Jesus answers the divorce test from creation rather than from the law's permission, quoting Genesis 1 and 2. Mark alone adds the case of a wife divorcing her husband, reflecting Roman law for his readers.
13.question: How does grounding a hard teaching in creation, rather than in rules, change how you receive it?

13.title: Like a Little Child
13.context: Children in the ancient world were received, not achievers; the blessing pictures the kingdom as gift. Jesus' indignation falls on the disciples who treated the children as interruptions.
13.question: What would receiving the kingdom like a child mean for the way you pray this week?

13.title: One Thing You Lack
13.context: Mark alone says Jesus looked at the man and loved him before the hard sentence. The camel and needle image is deliberate impossibility; the answer moves salvation out of human ability altogether.
13.question: If Jesus looked at you with love and named one thing you lack, what do you already know it would be?

13.title: A Hundredfold, with Persecutions
13.context: The third prediction is the most detailed: chief priests, Gentiles, mocking, spitting, flogging, killing, rising. Mark's hundredfold promise includes persecutions inside the blessing, not as an exception to it.
13.question: What have you actually received back, in this age, for what following Jesus has cost you?

13.title: A Ransom for Many
13.context: Bartimaeus is named, unlike most people healed in the Gospels, perhaps because he was known to Mark's first readers. His title for Jesus, Son of David, is the first public use of it in Mark.
13.question: The rich man and Bartimaeus both meet Jesus on the road. What made the difference in how their stories end?

14.title: Blessed Is He Who Comes
14.context: The colt and the cloaks and branches answer Zechariah 9:9. Mark's entry ends quietly: Jesus looks around the temple and leaves for the night, a detail only Mark records.
14.question: What does it say about Jesus that his first act on entering his capital is to inspect it and say nothing?

14.title: A House of Prayer for All the Nations
14.context: Mark sandwiches the fig tree around the temple action, his common device for letting one scene interpret another. The charge joins Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11.
14.question: Where might your own religious life have leaves, the profession, without the fruit it advertises?

14.title: Have Faith in God
14.context: The withered tree is discovered the next morning, from the roots. The prayer teaching that follows joins faith to forgiveness, as in the Lord's Prayer.
14.question: Is there a forgiveness you are holding back that Jesus would connect to your praying?

14.title: We Do Not Know
14.context: The delegation represents the Sanhedrin's three orders: chief priests, scribes, elders. Their deliberation is recorded in their own words, fearing heaven's verdict and the crowd's in turn.
14.question: When have you chosen 'we do not know' because the honest answer would cost you something?

15.title: The Stone the Builders Rejected
15.context: The vineyard picture comes from Isaiah 5, where the vineyard is Israel. The cornerstone quotation is Psalm 118:22-23, the same psalm that supplied the Hosanna of the entry.
15.question: How does the parable's owner, sending servant after servant and finally his son, describe God's patience with you?

15.title: Give to Caesar What Is Caesar's
15.context: The denarius bore Caesar's image and a blasphemous inscription calling him divine. The trap's two horns were treason to Rome or disloyalty to Israel; the answer refuses both.
15.question: What bears God's image in your life that must be rendered to God, the way Caesar's coin is rendered to Caesar?

15.title: The God of the Living
15.context: The Sadducees accepted only the Torah, so Jesus answers from Exodus 3, the burning bush. The scribe's response ranks love above sacrifice, echoing Hosea 6:6, and is the day's one honest exchange.
15.question: Which of the two great commandments is easier for you to keep in form, and which is God pressing on in fact?

15.title: All She Had to Live On
15.context: The widow's two lepta were the smallest coins in circulation, together worth a fraction of a denarius. The scene closes Jesus' public teaching in the temple; the scribes who devour widows' houses stand in the background of her gift.
15.question: What would giving out of poverty rather than surplus look like in one area of your life?

16.title: Not One Stone Left on Another
16.context: Herod's temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world, its stones enormous. The discourse is given to four disciples privately on the Mount of Olives, facing the temple across the valley.
16.question: What impressive and permanent thing in your world might Jesus regard with the same calm as these stones?

16.title: The Beginning of Birth Pains
16.context: The discourse warns first against deception, not against suffering. The promise that the gospel must be proclaimed to all nations is set inside the prediction of persecution, not after it.
16.question: How does knowing trouble is expected change the way you meet it when it comes?

16.title: Let the Reader Understand
16.context: The abomination of desolation quotes Daniel (Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11), and Mark's aside to the reader is his own voice breaking into the discourse. The flight instructions are urgent and unadorned.
16.question: What does it do to your reading of this chapter that Jesus insists some of it belongs to a specific generation's crisis?

16.title: Coming in the Clouds with Great Power and Glory
16.context: The darkened sun and falling stars draw on Isaiah 13 and 34 and Joel 2. The Son of Man coming in clouds quotes Daniel 7:13, where the movement is toward the Ancient of Days to receive a kingdom.
16.question: What does Jesus' certainty about his own words outlasting heaven and earth do to your confidence in them?

16.title: Keep Watch
16.context: The Son's confession that he does not know the day or hour is unique to Mark and Matthew's parallel. The four watches of the night named in the parable structure Mark's coming passion narrative, where the disciples will sleep instead.
16.question: In which watch of your life is watchfulness hardest, and what would keeping watch look like there?

17.title: She Has Done What She Could
17.context: Nard was an imported perfume from northern India, worth more than a year's wages. Mark does not name the woman; John names her as Mary of Bethany. Jesus' defense links her act to his burial, days before it.
17.question: What beautiful and impractical act of devotion might Jesus defend in you that practical voices call waste?

17.title: Judas Went to the Chief Priests
17.context: Mark gives Judas no stated motive and no fixed price in his account. The Passover preparations follow the pattern of the colt: instructions, a sign in the city, and everything found as Jesus said.
17.question: What stands out to you about how quietly Mark tells the betrayal next to the anointing's extravagance?

17.title: This Is My Blood of the Covenant
17.context: The covenant wording reaches back to Exodus 24:8, where Moses sprinkled blood to seal the covenant at Sinai. The betrayal is announced within the same meal, before the bread and cup.
17.question: How does eating this meal, knowing one at the table would betray him, shape what the meal means to you?

17.title: Before the Rooster Crows Twice
17.context: The scattering quotation is Zechariah 13:7. Mark alone specifies the rooster crowing twice, and his narrative will mark both crowings in the courtyard scene.
17.question: Where have you made Peter's promise, certain of your own strength, and what did the night teach you?

18.title: Abba, Father
18.context: Abba is the Aramaic family word for father, kept untranslated by Mark as at Galatians 4:6 and Romans 8:15. Gethsemane means oil press, a fitting name for the garden on the Mount of Olives.
18.question: In your hardest prayer, how do 'take this cup from me' and 'not what I will' live together?

18.title: The Spirit Is Willing, but the Body Is Weak
18.context: Jesus calls Peter by his old name, Simon, in the rebuke. The three who saw the glory on the mountain are the three who cannot stay awake in the garden.
18.question: When has sleep, in whatever form, won the hour you meant to give to watching and prayer?

18.title: Everyone Deserted Him and Fled
18.context: The young man in the linen cloth appears only in Mark, and readers since ancient times have wondered if it is the evangelist's own signature. The arrest fulfills Jesus' word that the sheep would be scattered.
18.question: What do you make of the fact that the Gospel's last follower to flee leaves naked, and that Mark kept the detail?

18.title: I Am
18.context: The high priest's question joins Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 in Jesus' answer. The court's difficulty was legal: witnesses disagreed, and the verdict finally rests on Jesus' own confession.
18.question: What does it cost you to answer plainly about who Jesus is when a plain answer invites a verdict?

18.title: He Broke Down and Wept
18.context: The courtyard scene interweaves with the trial inside, Mark's sandwich device: Jesus confesses under oath while Peter denies in the yard. The second crowing fulfills Mark's specific twice.
18.question: Where do you need the same mercy Peter needed, a Lord who named him again after the denials?

19.title: You Have Said So
19.context: Roman trials before a governor allowed accusers to present charges; the silence of the accused was unusual enough to amaze Pilate. The envy motive is Mark's own observation (15:10).
19.question: What does Jesus' silence under accusation teach you about when to answer and when not to?

19.title: Crucify Him
19.context: Barabbas is introduced as an insurrectionist and murderer; some manuscripts give his full name as Jesus Barabbas, though the BSB does not. The release custom is known only from the Gospels.
19.question: When have you felt the pressure Pilate felt, to satisfy a crowd against what you knew was right?

19.title: The King of the Jews
19.context: Simon of Cyrene's sons Alexander and Rufus are named as if known to the readers (compare Romans 16:13). The third hour is about nine in the morning; the lots for the garments recall Psalm 22:18.
19.question: What detail of the crucifixion road stays with you most, and why that one?

19.title: Truly This Man Was the Son of God
19.context: The cry from the cross is Psalm 22:1 in Aramaic. The veil's tearing is told without explanation, top to bottom. The centurion's confession is the first by any human in Mark since Peter's, and it comes from the executioner.
19.question: Why do you think Mark gives the Gospel's fullest confession to a Roman soldier at the foot of the cross?

19.title: Boldly Went to Pilate
19.context: Joseph of Arimathea's boldness is Mark's word; requesting a crucified man's body from Pilate was a public act. The women who watched are named as witnesses of both the death and the burial place.
19.question: What bold act for Jesus might your position, like Joseph's, uniquely enable?

20.title: Who Will Roll Away the Stone?
20.context: The women come to complete the anointing interrupted by the Sabbath. Tombs of the wealthy were sealed with rolling stones set in a groove, heavy enough to need several men.
20.question: What errand of love have you set out on without knowing how its biggest obstacle would move?

20.title: He Has Risen; He Is Not Here
20.context: The young man's message singles out Peter by name among the disciples. Galilee, where the ministry began, is named as the meeting place, fulfilling Jesus' word at the supper (14:28).
20.question: Why do you think the first resurrection message makes a point of saying 'and Peter'?

20.title: They Said Nothing to Anyone
20.context: Here the earliest manuscripts of Mark end, with the women fleeing in fear and the message undelivered by them. The verses that follow (9-20) are the church's received ending, printed in the BSB, and are told in the next scenes as they stand.
20.question: What does an ending in fear and silence, with the tomb already empty, say about who carries the news in the end?

20.title: They Did Not Believe It
20.context: The received ending reports two appearances and two disbelievings before the Eleven see Jesus themselves. Mary Magdalene is identified as the woman from whom seven demons had been driven out (compare Luke 8:2).
20.question: What does the repeated disbelief of the witnesses do to your own confidence in their testimony?

20.title: Go into All the World
20.context: The commission in the received ending is the widest in the Gospels. The ascension closes the book where its confession began: the Son of God, seated at the right hand of Power, as he told the council (14:62).
20.question: Mark's Gospel ends with ordinary people preaching everywhere and the Lord working through them. Where is your everywhere?
